<!-- The screenshots in figures/ were captured from run_app() with Demo mode
     left on, so they need no key and no network. Recapture them whenever the

`run_app()` opens a local Shiny app that drives the scopusflow workflow through
a browser tab, from describing a search to exporting the records, without
writing any R. It runs on your own machine, so your Scopus key never leaves it
and requests come from your own network. The app also serves as an introduction
to the package, because it writes every choice you make into a runnable R
script.

The code chunks in this article are shown but not evaluated, because running the
app needs a live server. The screenshots were taken from the running app with
Demo mode left on. Demo mode needs no key and no network, so everything they
show can be reproduced on your own machine in a minute.

## Launching the app

The app needs the suggested packages shiny, bslib and callr, and ggplot2 for the
plots. With those installed, one call opens it.

```{r}
library(scopusflow)
run_app()
```

By default, it listens only on `127.0.0.1`, so it is reachable from your own
machine alone. It also opens your browser at the address it prints. Passing
`launch.browser = FALSE` prevents this, and `port` fixes the port when you need
a stable address.

## Demo mode

Demo mode is switched on when the app opens, so you can try every step of the
workflow without a key. With it on, the harvest is replayed from the bundled
corpus, the live terminal still streams its per-cell progress, the tables and
plots still render, and the Compare topics tab still draws a figure. It is the
quickest way to learn where each control sits before you spend any quota.

The records come from `example_records`, a corpus of 138 published journal
articles bundled with the package. Every panel therefore works on the articles'
own titles, DOIs, journals and citation counts, and the by-year chart shows a
real publication curve with the shape the literature has. Scopus records may not
be redistributed, so the corpus is not a Scopus harvest. The corpus covers 2015
to 2024, and the year slider opens on that span. A year outside it is drawn from
the nearest year the corpus holds, and the live terminal says so for each such
year. Only the topic comparison is synthesised, because it counts whole
literatures and no set of records in hand holds those counts.

When you are ready for real results, paste your Scopus key into the field at
the top of the sidebar and switch Demo mode off. The key stays in the running
session and is never written into the generated script.

## Describing and sizing a search

The sidebar is where you describe the search. You enter your terms, choose which
field to search in, set a year range and pick the level of detail. Partitioning
by year is recommended and switched on by default, because it keeps each cell
under the API's offset ceiling, as with a partitioned `scopus_plan()` in code.

Check size runs a cheap count first, the same one `scopus_count()` performs, so
you can see how much a query would retrieve before committing to it. In demo
mode, it reports instead how many records it would draw from the bundled corpus.
The note it shows applies to the search on screen, so it goes as soon as the
terms, the field, the years, the detail or the cap change. Check size waits
while a harvest is running, since the app runs one job at a time.

Max records per cell is blank when the app opens, so the app sets no cap of its
own and each cell is retrieved up to the offset ceiling of 5000 records. A
number there caps each cell, or the whole search when partitioning is off,
which keeps a first look at a large search cheap. The generated script passes
it as `max_results`.

## Fetching, with a live terminal

Fetch records starts the harvest in a background process, so the app stays
responsive while it works. The Live terminal panel shows the worker's output,
streaming a line as each year-cell starts, and a progress bar counts the cells
already finished. Cancel ends the background process at once and abandons the
cell being fetched.

Internally, the app builds a `scopus_plan()` from your choices and hands it to
`scopus_fetch_plan()` with a cache directory and resume turned on. Each cell is
checkpointed as it completes, and a checkpoint is written to a temporary file
and renamed into place, so a cancelled run leaves the cache intact. Fetching the
same search again in the same tab, after Cancel or a failure, therefore resumes
from the cells already checkpointed and spends nothing on them.

Those checkpoints belong to the browser tab. Each tab keeps them in a temporary
directory of its own, removed when the tab closes. No search terms are left on
disk, and closing one tab never touches the harvest running in another. The
checkpoints also go when the app stops, so a harvest that has to outlast the
session, such as one stopped by the weekly quota, needs the script the app
writes. That script keeps its checkpoints under `scopus_cache_dir()`, in a
directory of the plan's own, and resumes from them each time it is run.

A note reads 'Demo plan: 10 year-cells; would draw 138 records from the bundled corpus.', and a label reads 'Fetching cell 8 of 10' above a progress bar at 70%. The expanded Live terminal below shows eight lines, one for each cell the run has reached, each reading 'Cell n/10: demo records for graphene supercapacitor' with its year, from 2015 to 2022.](figures/app-terminal.png)

## The reproducible code panel

The Reproducible code panel rewrites a runnable R script as you go to match
every choice you make: the query, the field, the year range, whether you
partition by year and the Compare topics options. Change a control and the
script updates at once, so you can see which argument each choice sets. The key
is never written into the script. The panel notes that it is read from the
`SCOPUS_API_KEY` environment variable, so a script you share carries the method
but not your credentials.

The script opens with a comment naming the scopusflow version that wrote it. A
script written in demo mode then says that the records on screen were replayed
from the bundled corpus. Its `scopus_fetch_plan()` call keeps the plan's
checkpoints in a directory of their own under `scopus_cache_dir()`, named from
the query and the years with a short hash added. Scripts for different searches
therefore never overwrite each other's cells. The records are saved before
anything is plotted, and the plot is drawn only where ggplot2 is installed. With
comparison terms entered, the script ends with the comparison, run over the same
years as in the app. Download script saves exactly what you see.

![The Reproducible code panel, holding the opening of the script the app has written from the choices in the sidebar. It starts with the comment '# scopusflow 0.4.0' and a demo-mode note saying that the records shown were replayed from example_records and that the script below is the live equivalent. Then come a library call, a scopus_plan() with the query, the years 2015 to 2024, the field and the yearly partition, and a scopus_count() to size the search. Last is a scopus_fetch_plan() whose cache directory lies under scopus_cache_dir() and is named graphene-supercapacitor-2015-2024 with a short hash added, with resume set. A comment records that the key is read from the SCOPUS_API_KEY environment variable and never written into the script.](figures/app-code.png)

## Reading the results

When the run finishes, the Results tabs show what it retrieved. Records shows a
table of titles, years, sources and citations. A line above it gives the number
of records the harvest holds, and says when the table shows only the first 25
of them. When a harvest fails, the app gives the reason in the worker's own
words.

By year draws the records per year through `autoplot()`, which traces the
publications per year when every record was retrieved. When a cap stopped a
cell, the bars count the records retrieved instead. The chart's caption says
so, and so do a note in the Retrieval panel and the search record. When the
years reach the year of the harvest, the caption also says that year was
incomplete when the records were retrieved.

Top sources and Top authors tally the most frequent of each with `scopus_top()`
and `plot_scopus_top()`. Under the `STANDARD` detail, the API sends the first
author of each record alone, so a note above the Top authors plot says that it
tallies first authors. Choosing `COMPLETE` gives every author. When a harvest
matched nothing, or its source titles or author names are all missing, the tab
says so where the figure would be.

Every figure is drawn by the same library functions you would call from a
script, so you can reproduce all of them from code. For screen readers, each
also carries a text alternative that names what it shows.

![The Results panel with tabs for Records, By year, Top sources, Top authors, Compare topics and Export. The Records tab is open, with a line reading '138 records (showing the first 25)' above the first rows of a table of titles, years, journals and citation counts from the demo harvest. The first row is a 2015 article on all-solid-state symmetric graphene supercapacitors, published in the Journal of Inorganic Materials, with one citation. The rows below it are likewise real articles from the bundled corpus.](figures/app-results.png)

## Comparing topics

The Compare topics tab measures how a set of sub-topics co-occur with your
search over time, as a share of it, with your search terms acting as the
reference topic. It retrieves no records. You enter comma-separated comparison
terms, optionally pick one to highlight, and toggle the stability band and
whether each topic's label carries its record count. Each term needs one count
request per year, and the reference topic one more, so two terms over six years
take 18 requests. The tab gives that number and advises fewer terms or years
above 80. With Partition by year off, the comparison covers the last six years.

In demo mode, the comparison is synthesised so you can see the figure offline. A
note under it says that its counts are illustrative, since the figure's own
caption names the Search API as its source. With a key, the tab calls
`scopus_compare_topics()` and draws the result with `plot_scopus_comparison()`,
the same figure the package produces.

## Exporting

Every result the app shows can be exported with one click. The records can be
saved as an RDS file, as a clean DOI list, and as BibTeX and RIS for a reference
manager such as Zotero or EndNote, drawn from `as_bibtex()` and `as_ris()`. They
can also be saved as a PRISMA-S search record in Markdown, drawn from
`scopus_search_report()`. In demo mode, that record names no search expression,
plan or retrieval time. It leaves out the phrase the corpus carries, which comes
from the OpenAlex search that produced the corpus and was never sent to Scopus.
The search record opens by saying that the records on screen were replayed from
the bundled corpus and that it describes no search that was run. The Comparison
download saves the comparison's underlying numbers as a CSV. Each button appears
once there is something for it to write, those for the records after a harvest
and the one for the comparison after a comparison. None of this contacts the API
again, because it works on results already in hand.

## Beyond the app

Anything you can do in the app you can also do from code, but the reverse does
not hold. The app covers planning, retrieval and the trend, top and comparison
analyses, and the package goes further. `scopus_intersections()` counts how a
set of named concepts and their intersections overlap in the literature, and
`plot_scopus_intersections()` draws the result. `scopus_abstract()` retrieves
abstract text and richer metadata than the Search API returns, and
`scopus_corpus()` builds on it to give a harvest author keywords and structured
references for use in other tools. For anything the app does not cover, the
downloaded script is the place to carry on from.
